title: The Book Without Diagrams: Turin, Berlin, and the Pantheon
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Turin, born in the Kingdom of Sardinia
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by MacTutor and by Treccani's Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani. No source reached gives the house, so the pin is the corpus-canonical Turin pair 45.0703, 7.6869, inherited byte-identical from pierre_simon_laplace.journey.json.
stops.campa: On the twenty-fifth of January a son is born in Turin to Giuseppe Francesco Lodovico Lagrangia, an officer of the Sardinian treasury, and to Teresa Grosso, daughter of a physician of Cambiano. He is registered Giuseppe Lodovico Lagrangia, first of eleven children, of whom two will live to be adults. The family is well connected and no longer rich: the father's speculations have gone through a considerable fortune. Turin has a court, a garrison and a university, and no mathematician anyone outside Piedmont has heard of. The father keeps his post at the treasury and the household stays where it is.
stops.quote: If I had been rich, I probably would not have devoted myself to mathematics.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Lagrange, quoted in MacTutor History of Mathematics, footnoted there to the Enciclopedia Italiana (1933); no primary letter or manuscript located, so the attribution is tradition
suggested_refs: The baptismal register of Turin for 25 January 1736, not consulted in this pass
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giuseppe Luigi Lagrange' (Luigi Pepe)

stops.name: Turin, the university and the turn from law
stops.date_confidence: Treccani has him enrolled at fourteen and directed toward law; MacTutor says College of Turin rather than university, and the two are not reconciled here. Month and day unrecorded, defaulted to January. Coordinates are the Palazzo dell'Universita at Via Po 17, 45.0693, 7.6888, per it.wikipedia; the research pool's 45.0672, 7.6879 is about 240 m off and is corrected here.
stops.campa: His father puts him to law. He reads Latin instead, and takes to Virgil and Cicero the way another boy takes to a trade, and finds the geometry of the ancients dry when he is finally shown it. He is fourteen when he enrolls. Then a paper of Edmond Halley on the uses of algebra in optics comes into his hands and he reads it through. Within a year, with no teacher, he has taught himself the analysis of his own century and is past everything Turin can set in front of him.
suggested_refs: Delambre's eloge of Lagrange, which reports the Halley episode from Lagrange's own later conversation; not verified against Delambre's text in this pass
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giuseppe Luigi Lagrange'

stops.name: Turin, the first printed letter
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by MacTutor and Treccani. He signs himself Luigi De la Grange Tournier, the first of the several forms of his name.
stops.campa: At eighteen he sends out his first mathematical work, a letter in Italian to Giulio Carlo Fagnano on an analogy between the binomial theorem and the successive derivatives of a product. He signs it Luigi De la Grange Tournier. He has also sent it to Leonhard Euler in Berlin. Within weeks he learns that the result is not his: Leibniz and Johann Bernoulli had it forty years before, in print, in a correspondence he had never seen. After this he does not put anything into print without first finding out what has already been done with it.
suggested_refs: The 23 July 1754 letter to Giulio Carlo Fagnano, Lagrange's first appearance in print
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giuseppe Luigi Lagrange'

stops.name: Turin, the letter to Euler
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor dates the letter 12 August 1755 and attests both the tautochrone results and the new method of maxima and minima. Location inferred: every source has him resident in Turin through 1755. The further detail that Euler held back his own work on the subject so that Lagrange could publish first is standard in the literature but was not verified against a source in this pass. The Euler Archive correspondence guide cited in the research dossier returned 404 when checked and is recorded here as unreachable rather than as support.
stops.campa: On the twelfth of August he writes to Berlin again, and this time the contents are his own. He has found a purely analytic way to handle problems of maxima and minima over curves, the tautochrone among them, replacing the geometrical constructions Euler had used with a calculus that runs on symbols alone. Euler will later give the subject its name, the calculus of variations. He reads the letter, sets aside his own work on the question so the young man in Turin can publish first, and writes back that the method leaves nothing to be desired. Lagrange is nineteen.
suggested_refs: The Euler-Lagrange correspondence, 1754-1775, in the Opera Omnia series IVA

stops.name: Turin, the artillery school
stops.date_confidence: the date is disputed and the rank was overstated in the research dossier. Treccani ('nominato assistente per il corso di matematica delle Reali Scuole di artiglieria') and it.wikipedia ('Sostituto del Maestro di Matematica') both give 26 September 1755 and an assistant post; MacTutor alone gives 28 September and the word professor. The 26th and the assistantship lead here, the 28th is recorded and not resolved. The pin 45.0648, 7.6747 could not be verified against any source for the eighteenth-century Regie Scuole d'Artiglieria; the schools sat by the Regio Arsenale on Via dell'Arsenale, nearer 45.068, 7.679, and the coordinate is carried as unverified.
stops.campa: He is made assistant for the mathematics course of the Royal Artillery Schools of Turin, his first paid work, at nineteen. The students are cadets who will lay guns; the assistant is the man who a month earlier corresponded with Euler as an equal. The tradition that he held a professorship at sixteen is a compression of this, and the documents do not support it. He teaches the elements to the cadets and sends his own work to Berlin. The salary is small and he holds the post, in one form or another, for eleven years.
suggested_refs: The registers of the Regie Scuole di Artiglieria, Turin, for September 1755
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giuseppe Luigi Lagrange'

stops.name: Turin, elected to Berlin at twenty
stops.date_confidence: the date is disputed between the two best secondary sources and is not resolved. MacTutor gives 2 September 1756; Treccani gives 5 October 1756 ('Lo stesso 5 ottobre il L. divenne associato dell'Academie royale des sciences et belles lettres de Berlin'). Read as September or October 1756. Euler's sponsorship is attested by MacTutor and by en.wikipedia. No primary Academy record was consulted.
stops.campa: Euler puts his name to the Berlin Academy and the Academy elects him a foreign member. He is twenty and has never left Piedmont. The mathematics that earns it is the variational method and a memoir on the propagation of sound, read in Berlin by the one man who has had his letters for two years and knows exactly what they are. Frederick the Great now holds, on paper, a Turinese assistant instructor he will spend the next decade trying to move to Berlin.
suggested_refs: The Berlin Academy's register of foreign associates for 1756
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giuseppe Luigi Lagrange'

stops.name: Turin, the society and the Miscellanea
stops.date_confidence: the founding year is attested by MacTutor and Treccani; no month is recorded and January is a default. The coordinates mark the Academy's later historic seat on Via Accademia delle Scienze, used because the earliest meeting rooms of the private society are not itemized in any source reached.
stops.campa: With the physician Giovanni Francesco Cigna and the young nobleman Giuseppe Angelo Saluzzo di Monesiglio he founds a private society for the sciences, meeting in rooms in Turin because the kingdom has no academy to meet in. Its journal is the Miscellanea Taurinensia, and its first volumes are largely him: the calculus of variations, the vibrating string, the propagation of sound, the theory of probability, mechanics. The society will become the Royal Academy of Sciences of Turin. Copies of the Miscellanea go out to Paris and to Berlin, where nobody has met its principal author.
suggested_refs: Miscellanea Taurinensia, volumes I-IV (1759-1766)
Accademia delle Scienze di Torino, membership record for Giuseppe Luigi Lagrange Tournier; not re-fetched in this pass
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giuseppe Luigi Lagrange'

segments.name: The Only Journey He Made for Curiosity

stops.name: Turin, setting out for Paris and London
stops.date_confidence: Treccani dates the departure to November 1763 and records the intention to see Paris and London; the day is not given and defaults to the first. Whether the London leg ever happened is not stated by Treccani and is left open here.
stops.campa: At twenty-seven he leaves Piedmont for the first time. He is travelling in the suite of the Marquis Caraccioli, the Neapolitan ambassador, and he means to see Paris and then cross to London. He has been elected to Berlin, printed in Turin, and read by Euler and d'Alembert, and he has met none of them. He carries with him a memoir on the libration of the Moon written for the prize the Paris Academy has set, and the manuscript is already in Paris ahead of him.
suggested_refs: The 1763-64 itinerary in Treccani's Dizionario Biografico entry
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giuseppe Luigi Lagrange'

stops.name: Paris, ill among the academicians
stops.date_confidence: the visit and the illness are attested by Treccani, which names d'Alembert and the diplomat Domenico Caracciolo as the men who saw him through it, and Clairaut, Condorcet and the abbe Nollet among those he met. Exact dates within November 1763 to May 1764 are not recorded; the day defaults to the first.
stops.campa: He reaches Paris in November and falls seriously ill there, an Italian of twenty-seven in a city he has read about for ten years and can barely leave his room in. D'Alembert and the ambassador Caracciolo nurse him through it. When he is well enough he meets Clairaut, Condorcet, the abbe Nollet, the whole apparatus of the Academy of Sciences, and they find that the letters had not exaggerated. D'Alembert writes to Turin about him that same month. He stays in Paris until the spring.
stops.quote: Monsieur de la Grange, a young geometer from Turin, has been here for six weeks. He has become very seriously ill and he needs, not financial help, for the Marquis de Caraccioli directed upon leaving for England that he should not be allowed to want for anything, but rather some sign of interest on the part of his native country. In him Turin possesses a treasure whose worth it perhaps does not know.
stops.quote_source: Jean le Rond d'Alembert, letter of November 1763, quoted in MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Joseph-Louis Lagrange'
suggested_refs: The d'Alembert-Lagrange correspondence, begun in Paris in 1763 and running to d'Alembert's death in 1783
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giuseppe Luigi Lagrange'

stops.name: Paris, the prize for the libration of the Moon
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor attests the 1764 prize on the libration of the Moon and a further prize in the competition on the inequalities of Jupiter's satellites associated with 1766. Neither award has a recorded month here, so both default to January; the 1766 award is folded into this stop rather than staged as a second scene at the same pin. The pin is the Louvre, seat of the Academie royale des sciences before 1793.
stops.campa: The Academie royale des sciences gives him its prize for a memoir explaining why the Moon keeps one face toward the Earth, a question the Academy had set and no one had answered with the three-body machinery it required. It is his first Paris prize and he is not yet a member of anything in France. Two years later the Academy sets the inequalities of Jupiter's satellites, and he wins that too, from Turin, without appearing. He does not travel to collect either one, and nobody in Paris has yet offered him a reason to.
suggested_refs: Lagrange, Recherches sur la libration de la Lune (1764), Academie royale des sciences prize memoir

stops.name: Ferney, at Voltaire's chateau
stops.date_confidence: Treccani attests the stop at Ferney on the homeward road, in the phrase 'si fermo a Ferney, per fare la conoscenza di Voltaire'; no month is recorded and January is a default. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from adam_smith.journey.json, whose 1765 stops pin the Chateau de Voltaire at 46.2574, 6.1036; the research pool's 46.2559, 6.1088 is not used.
stops.campa: On the road home he turns aside at Ferney, where Voltaire sits just inside the French border with Geneva behind him in case Paris ever moves. The reason given in the record is the plainest one: to make his acquaintance. Nothing of what passes at the table is written down by either man. He goes on over the Alps and is back in Turin by May, twenty-eight years old, carrying a Paris prize and the friendship of d'Alembert. The artillery school is still the only post his own country has given him.
suggested_refs: The Chateau de Voltaire at Ferney, where Lagrange called on the homeward journey of 1764
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giuseppe Luigi Lagrange'

segments.name: Berlin: Twenty-One Years at Euler's Desk

stops.name: Turin, leaving for good
stops.date_confidence: fr.wikipedia gives the departure as 21 August 1766, and MacTutor, en.wikipedia and fr.wikipedia agree on the year. The research dossier credited Treccani for the 1766 date, but Treccani as fetched prints the year 1767: 'Il 21 ag. 1767 il L. lascio Torino per non farvi piu ritorno.' The day and month are Treccani's, the year is not; 1766 is followed here and the discrepancy is recorded rather than resolved.
stops.campa: Euler has gone back to St Petersburg and Frederick II wants the best mathematician in Europe sitting in Berlin. D'Alembert, who had declined the post himself, presses Lagrange to take it. He had refused an earlier overture on a scruple that says most of what needs saying about him. Now the chair is empty, and Turin, which has had him for thirty years, has offered him nothing above the artillery school's salary to keep him. On the twenty-first of August he leaves the city he was born in. He does not come back to it.
stops.quote: It seems to me that Berlin would not be at all suitable for me while M Euler is there.
stops.quote_source: Lagrange, declining an earlier overture to Berlin, quoted in MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Joseph-Louis Lagrange'
suggested_refs: Frederick II's letters to Lagrange and d'Alembert on the succession to Euler, 1765-1766

stops.name: Paris, a call on d'Alembert
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor: 'he visited d'Alembert in Paris... before arriving in Berlin in October'. No date within the autumn is recorded and September is a default. MacTutor's fetched summary also named a stop with Caraccioli in London on this leg, which is almost certainly a garbled duplicate of the 1763 Paris episode with the Neapolitan diplomat; no 1766 London visit is carried here. Corpus-canonical Paris pin 48.8566, 2.3522.
stops.campa: The road to Berlin runs through Paris and he stops there to see d'Alembert, who three years ago sat by his sickbed and who has spent the interval writing to Frederick on his behalf. The two men have argued on paper about the vibrating string and the calculus of partial differences and will go on arguing for another seventeen years, in letters that never once turn cold. Then he goes east into a country whose language he does not speak, to a court that conducts its business in French.
suggested_refs: The d'Alembert-Lagrange correspondence, Oeuvres de Lagrange vol. XIII

stops.name: Berlin, director of the mathematics class
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor: 'succeeded Euler as Director of Mathematics at the Berlin Academy on 6 November 1766'. Treccani supplies the arrival on 21 October and the installation on 6 November, but its sentence sits inside a passage dated 1767, so it is cited here for day and month only and not for the year. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from leonard_euler.journey.json, which pins the Prussian Academy at 52.517, 13.3888; the research pool's 52.5177, 13.3944 is not used.
stops.campa: He arrives in Berlin on the twenty-first of October and is installed on the sixth of November as director of the mathematics class of the Royal Prussian Academy of Sciences. The desk is Euler's; so is the salary, six thousand francs, and so is the standing quarrel between the Academy's mathematicians and its philosophers that Euler left behind him. Lagrange will hold the post twenty-one years and will not once be drawn into a public dispute. The letters that used to run from Turin to Berlin now run out of Berlin. He is thirty years old.
suggested_refs: The Memoires de l'Academie royale des sciences et belles-lettres de Berlin, 1766-1787, which carry the bulk of his Berlin output
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giuseppe Luigi Lagrange'

stops.name: Berlin, the marriage to Vittoria Conti
stops.date_confidence: September 1767 per fr.wikipedia; MacTutor says only 'just under a year from the time he arrived in Berlin'. The precise day 6 September 1767, which the research dossier carried from secondary accounts, appears in none of MacTutor, Treccani, fr.wikipedia or en.wikipedia and is dropped here as false precision. The day defaults to the first.
stops.campa: Just under a year after arriving he marries his cousin Vittoria Conti, who had lived a long time in his father's house in Turin and who now comes north to keep his. He writes to d'Alembert about it in the register of a man reporting a decision rather than a feeling. He tells him too that he has no wish for children and that he thinks his own way of life unsuited to producing them. There will be none. They live in the middle of the city on Unter den Linden for twenty-one years.
stops.quote: My wife, who is one of my cousins and who even lived for a long time with my family, is a very good housewife and has no pretensions at all.
stops.quote_source: Lagrange, letter to d'Alembert, quoted in MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Joseph-Louis Lagrange'
suggested_refs: Treccani's account of the household 'nella centralissima Unter den Linden'
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giuseppe Luigi Lagrange'

stops.name: Berlin, four squares and Wilson's theorem
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor attests the four-square theorem to 1770 and Wilson's theorem to 1771. Neither has a recorded month; January is a default and the 1771 result is folded into this stop rather than given a second scene at the same pin.
stops.campa: He proves that every positive integer is the sum of four squares, a proposition Fermat had asserted and Euler had worked at for forty years without closing. The next year he proves Wilson's theorem, which had been stated in England without proof. Arithmetic is not his subject and he says so; he comes to it the way he comes to everything, because a stated thing is unproved and the machinery to prove it can be built. Both proofs go into the Nouveaux Memoires of an academy he runs in a language he never learned.
suggested_refs: Lagrange, Demonstration d'un theoreme d'arithmetique, Nouveaux Memoires de l'Academie de Berlin (1770)
gauss.journey.json, whose 1792 and 1801 stops record Gauss reading Lagrange's arithmetic on his own and then gathering it into the Disquisitiones

stops.name: Berlin, the resolvents
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor dates the Reflexions sur la resolution algebrique des equations to 1770; no month is recorded and January is a default. The stop shares its date with the arithmetic stop above because both results fall in the same year and the sources give no finer ordering.
stops.campa: In the Reflexions sur la resolution algebrique des equations he asks not how to solve the cubic and the quartic, which is known, but why the known methods work, and he answers by watching what happens to a function of the roots when the roots are permuted among themselves. The resolvent of a fifth-degree equation, he finds, comes out of degree six: the method that lowered the others raises this one. He does not conclude that the quintic is unsolvable. He leaves the machinery in the open, and it is the machinery, not the conclusion, that outlives him.
suggested_refs: Lagrange, Reflexions sur la resolution algebrique des equations, Nouveaux Memoires de l'Academie de Berlin (1770-1771)

stops.name: Berlin, the three-body problem
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor attests the 1772 Paris prize on the three-body problem, shared with Euler, and the Essai sur le Probleme des Trois Corps. NASA's public explainer on Lagrange points credits Lagrange by name with the five equilibrium solutions. The prize was awarded in Paris and the work done in Berlin; the stop is pinned where the work was done. No month recorded, January defaults.
stops.campa: The Paris Academy sets the three-body problem and splits the prize between Euler and Lagrange, master and successor, on the same question. Lagrange's Essai finds exact solutions in which three bodies hold a fixed shape while they move, one of them at the apex of an equilateral triangle standing on the other two. No approximation and no series enter into it. For the rest of his life the result is treated as an elegant curiosity, a solution in celestial mechanics with nothing known in the sky to match it. He gives no indication of thinking otherwise about it himself.
suggested_refs: Lagrange, Essai sur le Probleme des Trois Corps (1772)
NASA, 'What Is a Lagrange Point?', science.nasa.gov, which names the five points after him

stops.name: Berlin, the prizes keep arriving from Paris
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor attests a 1774 prize on the secular acceleration of the Moon and a prize on the perturbations of comets which it dates to 1780; the research dossier dates the cometary competition to 1778. The gap is probably competition year against decision year and is not resolved here. The stop is dated to MacTutor's 1780 and carries both awards. No months recorded.
stops.campa: In 1774 the Academy of Sciences of a country he does not live in gives him its prize for the secular acceleration of the Moon, and again a few years later for the perturbations that comets suffer from the planets. He is a paid servant of Frederick II and the standing champion of the French Academy's competitions, and nobody in either capital finds this strange. The lunar and planetary memoirs of these years are the working half of his life; the other half is a manuscript he shows to no one.
suggested_refs: The Paris Academy prize memoirs of 1774 and 1778-1780, in Oeuvres de Lagrange vol. VI

stops.name: Berlin, the letter to Laplace
stops.date_confidence: the letter is dated 15 September 1782 in MacTutor, which quotes it. It is contemporary evidence that the Mecanique analytique was substantially finished six years before it was printed.
stops.campa: He writes to Pierre-Simon Laplace in Paris, twelve years his junior and the only other man alive who can read him at speed. They have been corresponding since Laplace's first paper came out in the Miscellanea Taurinensia, and they will end as colleagues on the same committees in the same city. The book is done, or nearly done: the whole of mechanics on one principle, worked out on paper over fifteen Berlin years. He has no publisher in Prussia and no urgency about finding one. He puts the manuscript back in the trunk and returns to the memoirs.
stops.quote: I have almost completed a 'Traite de mecanique analytique', based uniquely on the principle of virtual velocities; but, as I do not yet know when or where I shall be able to have it printed, I am not rushing to put the finishing touches to it.
stops.quote_source: Lagrange, letter to Laplace, 15 September 1782, quoted in MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Joseph-Louis Lagrange'
suggested_refs: The Lagrange-Laplace correspondence, Oeuvres de Lagrange vol. XIV

stops.name: Berlin, Vittoria dies
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor and Treccani attest the death in 1783 after a long illness through which Lagrange nursed her; no month is recorded and January is a default. The added detail in the research dossier, that a copy of the not-yet-printed Mecanique analytique lay unopened for two years, is later memorial anecdote and is not carried as a claim.
stops.campa: Vittoria dies after a long illness he has nursed her through himself, refusing to leave the house. They had been married sixteen years and had no children. He is forty-seven. He stops working and stops answering letters, and tells the correspondents who do reach him that mathematics no longer interests him and that he suspects it never really did. D'Alembert, who might have pulled him out of it, dies in Paris the same year. Frederick II has three years to live. Almost nothing comes off Lagrange's desk for the next four.
suggested_refs: Treccani's account of the illness and the collapse that followed
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giuseppe Luigi Lagrange'

stops.name: Berlin, the leave granted
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor's chronology reads '18 May 1787: Left Berlin for Paris', and fr.wikipedia independently gives the departure as 18 May 1787 and the arrival in Paris as 29 July 1787. The research dossier hedged this as possibly an arrival date; the hedge is not supported by the source and is dropped. Frederick II's death on 17 August 1786 is dated to the day in the dossier from secondary sources; MacTutor gives only the year.
stops.campa: Frederick dies in August 1786 and the court that replaces him has no use for a silent Italian who has published nothing much since his wife died. The offers arrive from everywhere at once: Naples, Turin, Paris. Louis XVI offers a pension, lodging in the Louvre, and membership of the Academie des sciences with no duties attached. Lagrange asks the Prussian Academy for an honourable discharge and gets it, keeping his Berlin salary as a pension. On the eighteenth of May he leaves the city after twenty-one years.
suggested_refs: The Prussian Academy's act of honourable discharge, May 1787

segments.name: Paris, and the Book Without Diagrams

stops.name: Paris, pensionnaire veteran
stops.date_confidence: fr.wikipedia gives the arrival in Paris as 29 July 1787; Treccani dates his admission to the Academie as pensionnaire veteran to 13 June 1787, which is before he arrived and therefore an election in absentia. The research dossier's 'May 1787' for the Paris arrival confuses the departure with the arrival and is corrected here. The pin is the Louvre, seat of the Academie royale des sciences and of the lodging granted him.
stops.campa: He reaches Paris at the end of July, having been elected to the Academie six weeks before he got there. The rank is pensionnaire veteran: full pay and no obligations of any kind. He is fifty-one, a widower, and by his own account finished. The pension and the rooms are the terms Louis XVI had offered him while he was still in Berlin. The rooms are connected with the Louvre and he keeps to them. Visitors find a famous mathematician with no appetite and no plans, and a manuscript in a trunk that he has not opened in five years.
suggested_refs: The registers of the Academie royale des sciences for 13 June 1787
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giuseppe Luigi Lagrange'

stops.name: Paris, the Mecanique analytique
stops.date_confidence: the 1788 first edition through Veuve Desaint is attested by MacTutor and Treccani; no month is recorded and January is a default. The often-repeated detail that Legendre saw the volume through the press was not verified in this pass and is not carried in the prose. Corpus-canonical Paris pin 48.8566, 2.3522, inherited byte-identical from pierre_simon_laplace.journey.json and simeon_denis_poisson.journey.json.
stops.campa: The manuscript from the trunk is printed in Paris while he takes no interest in it, and he does not open the presentation copy for two years. What is in it is the whole of statics and dynamics since Newton, reduced to one principle, virtual velocities, and carried out in generalized coordinates that need not be lengths or angles or anything a hand can draw. Mechanics stops being a branch of geometry in this book and becomes a branch of analysis. He says so himself, at the head of the volume, before the reader has reached a single equation.
stops.quote: One will not find figures in this work. The methods that I expound require neither constructions, nor geometrical or mechanical arguments, but only algebraic operations, subject to a regular and uniform course.
stops.quote_source: Lagrange, Avertissement to the Mecanique analytique (Paris, 1788), quoted in MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Joseph-Louis Lagrange'
suggested_refs: Lagrange, Mecanique analytique (Paris: Veuve Desaint, 1788)
Analytical Mechanics, trans. A. Boissonnade and V. N. Vagliente (Kluwer, 1997), the first full English version, confirmed in the OpenLibrary catalogue
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giuseppe Luigi Lagrange'

stops.name: Paris, the commission on weights and measures
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor attests the appointment in May 1790 and names Borda, Condorcet, Lavoisier, Laplace and Monge as colleagues, with Lagrange favouring decimal division. The day is not recorded and defaults to the first. pierre_simon_laplace.journey.json carries the same commission from the other side and records Laplace's removal from it by the Committee of Public Safety in December 1793.
stops.campa: The Assembly appoints a commission to fix the measures of France by nature instead of by custom, and he sits on it with Borda, Condorcet, Lavoisier, Laplace and Monge. The argument is about the base. Twelve has more divisors and the merchants want it; eleven is proposed by someone who wants a prime so that nobody can subdivide at all. Lagrange holds out for ten and gets it, and the decimal metric system that comes out of the room is his in this one respect completely. Within four years two of the men at that table are dead by the state.
suggested_refs: The proces-verbaux of the Commission des poids et mesures, 1790-1799

stops.name: Paris, the second marriage
stops.date_confidence: the day is disputed and mis-sourced in the research dossier. Treccani gives 24 May 1792; it.wikipedia gives 31 May 1792 with a notarial contract of 3 June. en.wikipedia carries neither day, so the dossier's attribution of 31 May to en.wikipedia is wrong and is corrected here. The day is left unresolved and defaults to the first of May. Adelaide Le Monnier's dates, 1767-1833, are established by Sarton, Taton and Beaujouan in the Revue d'histoire des sciences (1950), making her twenty-four or twenty-five and him fifty-six.
stops.campa: Renee-Francoise-Adelaide Le Monnier, daughter of the astronomer Pierre-Charles Le Monnier, is twenty-four and proposes the marriage herself. He is fifty-six, sunk in the depression that has not lifted since Berlin, and he accepts. She refuses to be left behind by him in anything: she learns enough of his subject to talk to him about it and gets him out of the apartment, and everyone who saw them credits her with giving him back the will to work. The royal family signs the contract in May 1792. What she wanted with him at that age is not something anyone who knew them wrote down.
suggested_refs: G. Sarton, R. Taton and G. Beaujouan, 'Documents nouveaux concernant Lagrange', Revue d'histoire des sciences 3 (1950), persee.fr, which used family papers held in Turin to correct the later gossip about this marriage
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giuseppe Luigi Lagrange'
Sarton, Taton and Beaujouan, Revue d'histoire des sciences 3 (1950)

stops.name: Paris, the academies shut and the foreigners listed
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor attests the suppression of the learned societies on 8 August 1793. The month of the law on foreigners born in enemy countries is disputed: MacTutor says September 1793, en.wikipedia says October. MacTutor is explicit about the agent, which the research dossier had dropped: 'Lavoisier intervened on behalf of Lagrange, who certainly fell under the terms of the law, and he was granted an exception.' Both events are carried at the one pin, the Louvre, where the Academie sat.
stops.campa: On the eighth of August the Convention suppresses the Academie des sciences along with every other learned society in France. A few weeks later a law orders the arrest of all foreigners born in enemy countries, and Lagrange, a subject of the King of Sardinia who has never taken French nationality, falls squarely inside it. Lavoisier intervenes for him by name and the exception is granted. He is a Piedmontese pensioner of a dead king, kept in Paris by a chemist who has eight months to live.
stops.quote: I believe that, in general, one of the first principles of every wise man is to conform strictly to the laws of the country in which he is living, even when they are unreasonable.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Lagrange in MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Joseph-Louis Lagrange'; presented there without a letter date or archival citation and not confirmed against any primary document in this pass
suggested_refs: The decree of 8 August 1793 suppressing the academies; the law on foreigners of September or October 1793

stops.name: Place de la Revolution, Lavoisier's head
stops.date_confidence: the execution is dated 8 May 1794. Whether Lagrange was present is not established by any source reached, and the stop is pinned at the scaffold because that is where the event happened, not because his attendance is attested. The remark is the most repeated sentence anyone ever put in his mouth and its exact French wording and first documentary appearance have not been traced; a variant reading runs 'cut off that head, but France may not produce another like it in a century'. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from louis_xvi.journey.json, which pins the Place de la Revolution at 48.8648, 2.3268.
stops.campa: Lavoisier is tried in the morning and guillotined in the afternoon with twenty-seven other farmers-general, eight months after the intervention that kept Lagrange in France. The Commission of Weights and Measures loses the man who had been its chemist and the metric system goes on being built without him. Whether Lagrange stood in the square that afternoon is established by nothing. What he said when he heard the news is recorded in no document anyone has produced since, and it comes down in more than one wording.
stops.quote: It took only a moment to cause this head to fall and a hundred years will not suffice to produce its like.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Lagrange on Lavoisier's execution, quoted in MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Joseph-Louis Lagrange'; no contemporaneous documentation of the French wording located
suggested_refs: The judgment of the Revolutionary Tribunal against the farmers-general, 8 May 1794
sources: Wikiquote, 'Joseph-Louis Lagrange', for the variant wording

stops.name: Paris, first professor of analysis
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor gives the foundation of the Ecole centrale des travaux publics on 11 March 1794 and its opening in December 1794; the day of opening is not recorded and defaults to the first. The school's first quarters were in the Palais Bourbon. The research pool's pin 48.8606, 2.3183 sits about 155 m short of the Palais Bourbon; the coordinate used here, 48.8608, 2.3183, is inherited byte-identical from joseph_fourier.journey.json's stop for this same chair.
stops.campa: The Republic needs engineers and founds a school to make them, in the Palais Bourbon, and Lagrange is its first professor of analysis. He is fifty-eight. The intake is a few hundred boys chosen by competition out of the whole of France, and they get the calculus from the man who wrote the Mecanique analytique, delivered in a weak voice with an Italian accent, at an altitude most of them cannot reach. His lecture courses here will become two books. The school is renamed the Ecole polytechnique the following year.
suggested_refs: The Palais Bourbon, first premises of the Ecole centrale des travaux publics, December 1794

stops.name: Paris, the Ecole normale de l'an III
stops.date_confidence: fr.wikipedia, 'Ecole normale de l'an III', fixes the session at 1 pluviose an III to 30 floreal an III, that is 20 January to 19 May 1795, in an amphitheatre of the Museum national d'histoire naturelle. MacTutor has Lagrange teaching elementary mathematics there and Laplace sharing the mathematics with him; the research dossier omitted Laplace. Fourier's attendance, which the dossier's writer could not verify, is attested by MacTutor through joseph_fourier.journey.json. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from joseph_fourier.journey.json and pierre_simon_laplace.journey.json (48.8416, 2.3622); the research pool's 48.844, 2.3588 is not used.
stops.campa: The Republic gathers provincial schoolmasters into an amphitheatre at the Jardin des Plantes and has the best men in France lecture at them for four months. Lagrange shares the mathematics with Laplace and begins at the beginning, arithmetic and algebra, for an audience mostly incapable of following him past the first hour. On the benches sits Joseph Fourier, twenty-six, lately out of a prison cell, who writes down what the lecturer sounds like. The school closes on the nineteenth of May.
stops.quote: His voice is very feeble, at least in that he does not become heated; he has a very pronounced Italian accent and pronounces the s like z. The students, of whom the majority are incapable of appreciating him, give him little welcome, but the professors make amends for it.
stops.quote_source: Joseph Fourier on Lagrange's lectures at the Ecole normale, 1795, quoted in MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Joseph-Louis Lagrange'
suggested_refs: The published Seances des Ecoles normales, an III, which print the mathematics lectures as delivered

stops.name: Paris, the Bureau des longitudes and the new Institut
stops.date_confidence: fr.wikipedia, 'Bureau des longitudes': created by the law of 25 June 1795 and first convened on 6 July 1795 in a room of the Petit Luxembourg, with Lagrange a founding member as geometre and its second president from September 1795. The research dossier's claim that the Paris Observatory was the Bureau's seat is contradicted by the same article: the Observatory was placed under the Bureau's oversight from 1795 to 1854. Coordinates for the Petit Luxembourg inherited byte-identical from pierre_simon_laplace.journey.json (48.8489, 2.3369). Membership of the mathematical class of the Institut national, founded the same year in the Louvre, is folded into this stop; its month is not established here.
stops.campa: A law of messidor creates one body to hold the astronomy, the navigation, the geodesy and the timekeeping of the Republic, and on the sixth of July it sits for the first time in a room of the Petit Luxembourg. Lagrange is a founding geometer and takes the presidency in September. The same year the Institut national replaces the academies the Convention had abolished two years earlier, in the Louvre, and he is elected to its mathematical class. He is fifty-nine and sits in both bodies from their first sessions.
suggested_refs: The law of 7 messidor an III establishing the Bureau des longitudes
The Petit Luxembourg, where the Bureau first met on 6 July 1795

stops.name: Paris, the chair given up
stops.date_confidence: joseph_fourier.journey.json states from MacTutor that Lagrange gave up the chair of analysis and mechanics at the Ecole polytechnique in 1797 and Fourier was appointed to succeed him. fr.wikipedia gives his Polytechnique professorship as running 1794-1799. The two are not reconciled here: he may have kept other teaching after handing over the chair, and the Bugge account of 1799 below has him still lecturing in the building. No month is recorded and January is a default.
stops.campa: He gives up the chair of analysis and mechanics at the Ecole polytechnique, the most exacting mathematical teaching post in France, and it goes to Joseph Fourier, who two years earlier had been sitting in the amphitheatre at the Jardin des Plantes taking notes on his accent. Fourier is twenty-nine and has been out of a prison cell for three years. Lagrange is sixty-one and does not stop coming to the school. The two of them will sit at the same committee table again in 1807, on opposite sides of it.
suggested_refs: The Ecole polytechnique's registers of instruction for 1797

stops.name: Paris, calculus without infinitesimals
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor attests the Theorie des fonctions analytiques to 1797, the Resolution des equations numeriques to 1798, and the Lecons sur le calcul des fonctions to 1800; all three grew out of the Polytechnique courses. No months are recorded and January is a default; the later two volumes are folded into this stop rather than staged separately at the same pin.
stops.campa: He tries to put the calculus on a footing that needs no infinitely small quantity, no vanishing ratio, and no limit: every function is to be expanded in a power series, and the derivative is to be read off from the coefficients. The word derivative is his, and so is the notation with the prime. The programme itself does not survive; the series he needs do not always converge and he has not the machinery to say when they do. Two more volumes follow, on numerical equations and on the calculus of functions, out of the same lectures.
stops.quote: The principles of the differential calculus, freed from all consideration of the infinitely small or vanishing quantities, of limits or fluxions, and reduced to the algebraic analysis of finite quantities.
stops.quote_source: Lagrange, Theorie des fonctions analytiques (Paris, 1797), title page and preface, quoted in MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Joseph-Louis Lagrange'
suggested_refs: Lagrange, Theorie des fonctions analytiques (1797); Resolution des equations numeriques (1798); Lecons sur le calcul des fonctions (1800)
augustin_louis_cauchy.journey.json, whose 1810 stop has Cauchy carrying the Theorie des fonctions analytiques to Cherbourg as one of four books

stops.name: Paris, a Dane in the lecture room
stops.date_confidence: Thomas Bugge's remark is dated 1799 by MacTutor, which quotes it from the Danish astronomer's travel account of revolutionary Paris. The day and month are not recorded and default to January. Simeon Denis Poisson entered the Ecole polytechnique in 1798, first in the entrance examination, and simeon_denis_poisson.journey.json records that Lagrange and Laplace were both teaching in the building that year.
stops.campa: Thomas Bugge, director of the Copenhagen observatory, comes to Paris to see what the Republic has made of the sciences and sits in on the mathematics at the Ecole polytechnique. He goes away impressed and unconvinced that the arrangement works. In the same rooms a poor boy from the Loiret, Simeon Denis Poisson, has just come first in the entrance examination and is taught that year by Lagrange and by Laplace, in the same building, on the same subject.
stops.quote: Whatever this great man says, deserves the highest degree of consideration, but he is too abstract for youth.
stops.quote_source: Thomas Bugge on Lagrange's lectures at the Ecole polytechnique, 1799, quoted in MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Joseph-Louis Lagrange'
suggested_refs: Thomas Bugge, Travels in the French Republic (English edition, 1801)

stops.name: Palais du Luxembourg, the Senat conservateur
stops.date_confidence: fr.wikipedia dates the appointment to 4 nivose an VIII, that is 25 December 1799; Treccani gives 24-25 December 1799. The research pool's coordinate 48.8462, 2.3372 is about 245 m too far south and is the Pantheon's latitude, apparently copied from the Pantheon row; the Palais du Luxembourg is at 48.8484, 2.3372 and the pin is corrected here.
stops.campa: Six weeks after the coup of 18 Brumaire, Bonaparte names him to the Senat conservateur, the body that is to guard a constitution nobody expects to be guarded. The salary is large and the duties are ceremonial. Lagrange is sixty-three and has now been paid by a king of Sardinia, a king of Prussia, a king of France, a republic, a directory and a consul, without changing what he does at his desk in the morning. He votes as the others vote and says nothing in the chamber that anybody wrote down.
suggested_refs: The senatus-consultes of the Senat conservateur, 1799-1814
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giuseppe Luigi Lagrange'

stops.name: Paris, at the Cauchy table
stops.date_confidence: tradition, not document. augustin_louis_cauchy.journey.json carries the story from Belhoste's biography and flags it in its own prose as tradition; the address of the Cauchy household is not recorded, and the coordinate 48.8462, 2.3466 is inherited byte-identical from that file, where it pins the Ecole Centrale du Pantheon rather than the family lodging. No month is recorded and January is a default. That file also states that Lagrange has no atlas journey; the present file supersedes the statement.
stops.campa: He calls on Louis-Francois Cauchy, a former police lieutenant-general of Paris turned secretary of the Senate, and sees the son, thirteen years old, at work on something. The advice he gives the father is to keep the boy off mathematics until he has his Latin and Greek, on the ground that a mind used too early is used up. The father obeys. The boy goes to the Ecole Centrale du Pantheon for two years of grammar and prosody and comes back to the subject at fifteen. Nothing in the story is documented; it comes down through the family.
suggested_refs: B. Belhoste, Augustin-Louis Cauchy: A Biography (1991), which carries the family tradition

stops.name: Institut de France, the committee that refuses Fourier
stops.date_confidence: the reading date is attested to the day through joseph_fourier.journey.json and pierre_simon_laplace.journey.json, both sourced to MacTutor and en.wikipedia; the committee was Lagrange, Laplace, Monge and Lacroix, and the refusal to publish is dated 1808. simeon_denis_poisson.journey.json records that a summary of Fourier's theory then appeared in the Bulletin de la Societe Philomatique signed with the letter P. Institut pin 48.8566, 2.3376 inherited byte-identical from augustin_louis_cauchy.journey.json, evariste_galois.journey.json and joseph_fourier.journey.json.
stops.campa: Fourier reads his memoir on the propagation of heat in solid bodies to the Institute on the twenty-first of December, and it goes to a committee of four: Lagrange, Laplace, Monge, Lacroix. Lagrange will not accept the trigonometric series. The objection is not stupid; the convergence Fourier assumes is not proved and will not be proved for decades. He had taught this man in the amphitheatre at the Jardin des Plantes and handed him his own chair. He never withdraws the objection, and the memoir stays unpublished while he lives.
suggested_refs: The committee report on Fourier's 1807 memoir, Institut national, mathematical class

stops.name: Paris, count of the Empire
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor and Treccani attest the grand officership of the Legion d'honneur and the countship of the Empire in 1808; the letters patent were not fetched in this pass and no month is recorded, so January is a default. pierre_simon_laplace.journey.json dates Laplace's own countship to 24 April 1808. The Royal Society election is 1791 per fr.wikipedia, not 1806: en.wikipedia's sentence is ambiguously punctuated and the 1806 governs the Royal Swedish Academy alone, an error carried in the research dossier and corrected here.
stops.campa: Napoleon makes him grand officer of the Legion d'honneur and comte de l'Empire. He is seventy-two and has been decorated by every regime that has governed France in his lifetime, which is four. Laplace is made a count in the same year. The Emperor liked to talk to him and to bring visitors to look at him, and Lagrange sat through it with the same courtesy he gave the artillery cadets in Turin. He has been a Fellow of the Royal Society since 1791 and a foreign member of the Swedish academy since 1806.
suggested_refs: The letters patent creating Lagrange comte de l'Empire, 1808, not consulted in this pass
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giuseppe Luigi Lagrange'

stops.name: Rue du Faubourg-Saint-Honore, the revision
stops.date_confidence: the source was misattributed in the research dossier: MacTutor's biography contains nothing about a revision or a second edition. en.wikipedia gives 1810-1813 for the revision of the Mecanique analytique and states that about two thirds was finished before his death, with volume one appearing in 1811 and volume two posthumously in 1815. The dossier's citation to MacTutor is dropped. His address is given by Treccani as the rue du Faubourg-Saint-Honore, commonly cited as number 128 or 134; later renumbering accounts for the variation and the pin approximates the block.
stops.campa: At seventy-four he goes back through the Mecanique analytique line by line for a second edition, twenty-two years after the first, working in the Empire-style apartment on the rue du Faubourg-Saint-Honore, at a number given as 128 in some accounts and 134 in others because the street was renumbered later. The first volume comes out in 1811. He gets about two thirds of the way through the second and does not finish it; it is printed in 1815 by other hands. There are still no figures in it.
suggested_refs: Lagrange, Mecanique analytique, second edition, vol. I (1811) and vol. II (1815, posthumous)
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giuseppe Luigi Lagrange'

stops.name: Rue du Faubourg-Saint-Honore, the last honour and the death
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor dates the Grand Croix of the Ordre imperial de la Reunion to 3 April 1813 and the death to 10 April 1813 in Paris; Treccani and en.wikipedia agree on the death. The nature of the final illness is not documented in any source reached. The two events, a week apart at the same address, are carried at the one pin.
stops.campa: On the third of April Napoleon sends him the Grand Cross of the Imperial Order of the Reunion, the last decoration of a life that collected them from four regimes. He is seventy-seven and has been failing for months. He receives visitors in the days that follow and talks to them about his own death without any apparent distress, as a fact in the same class as all the others he has spent his life stating plainly. On the tenth of April he dies at home on the rue du Faubourg-Saint-Honore, seven days after the ribbon arrives. What killed him is not recorded anywhere.
suggested_refs: The death certificate of Joseph-Louis Lagrange, Paris, 10 April 1813, not consulted in this pass
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Giuseppe Luigi Lagrange'

stops.name: The Pantheon, the tomb of a senator

The inscription is transcribed from en.wikipedia. Pantheon pin 48.8462, 2.3464 is the corpus-canonical pair, used in rene_descartes.journey.json for the Convention's 1793 proposal to move Descartes there.
stops.campa: He is buried in the Pantheon with a state funeral, and the inscription over him lists the offices before it gets to the mathematics, because the offices are what the Empire is burying: senator, count of the Empire, grand officer of the Legion of Honour, grand cross of the Order of the Reunion, member of the Institute and of the Bureau of Longitudes. Then the two dates, born in Turin on the twenty-fifth of January 1736, died in Paris on the tenth of April 1813. The word mathematician does not appear on the stone.
stops.quote: Joseph Louis Lagrange. Senator. Count of the Empire. Grand Officer of the Legion of Honour. Grand Cross of the Imperial Order of the Reunion. Member of the Institute and the Bureau of Longitude. Born in Turin on 25 January 1736. Died in Paris on 10 April 1813.

stops.name: The Eiffel Tower, one of the seventy-two names
stops.date_confidence: the inscription of seventy-two names of French scientists and engineers on the first stage of the tower dates from its completion for the Exposition Universelle of 1889; no month applies and January is a default. Lagrange's inclusion is attested by en.wikipedia and by the fr.wikipedia list of the seventy-two names. The coordinate 48.8584, 2.2945 is the pair used in pierre_simon_laplace.journey.json; joseph_fourier.journey.json and rene_hauy.journey.json use 48.8583, 2.2945, and the one-digit divergence is recorded rather than resolved.
stops.campa: Seventy-six years after his funeral the Third Republic puts up an iron tower for a world's fair and writes seventy-two names around the first stage, the scientists and engineers of the century that France means to claim as its own. LAGRANGE is one of them, in capitals, between the mathematicians and the chemists of his own generation. He was born a subject of the King of Sardinia, kept his Italian accent to the end of his life, and never took French nationality. The tower was put up as a temporary structure for the exposition and was meant to be taken down after twenty years.

stops.name: Paris, the rue Lagrange
stops.date_confidence: fr.wikipedia, 'Rue Lagrange': the street was cut in 1887 to carry the rue Monge through to the quai, and formally named for Lagrange on 18 April 1890; it runs from the quai de Montebello to the rue Frederic-Sauton in the fifth arrondissement. Coordinates 48.8508, 2.3483 from the same article; the research pool's 48.8496, 2.3477 is about 135 m off and is corrected here.
stops.campa: A street is cut through the old quarter behind Notre-Dame in 1887 to bring the rue Monge down to the river, driven through the medieval lanes the way the whole of that quarter was driven through in those decades. In April 1890 it is given his name. It runs from the quai de Montebello to the rue Frederic-Sauton, in the fifth arrondissement, a short walk uphill from the Pantheon he lies in, through a quarter he had no particular connection with while he was alive. It is about three hundred metres long.
suggested_refs: The municipal decree of 18 April 1890 naming the rue Lagrange

stops.name: Turin, the Via Lagrange and the disputed name
stops.date_confidence: no source reached gives the year the Turin street was named, and the date is set only to order the segment after the Paris street; it should not be quoted as a fact. en.wikipedia and fr.wikipedia both attest the street and that it runs past the site of his birthplace. The Accademia delle Scienze di Torino membership record, which Italian scholarship uses to anchor his Piedmontese identity, was not re-fetched in this pass and is carried on the research dossier's citation alone.
stops.campa: Turin names a street after him too, running past the house where he was born, and Italian scholarship keeps his membership record filed under Giuseppe Luigi Lagrange Tournier. France buried him in the Pantheon and put him on the tower as one of its own. He was baptised Lagrangia, published first in Italian, signed himself De la Grange Tournier at eighteen, worked twenty-one years for a Prussian king in French, and died a count of a French empire without ever changing nationality. The year Turin put his name on the street is not recorded in anything reached here.
suggested_refs: Accademia delle Scienze di Torino, membership record for Giuseppe Luigi Lagrange Tournier, accademiadellescienze.it; not verified in this pass
